comment.value:
This paper introduces the LISAt dataset and benchmark for language-instructed video action segmentation. The dataset is well-motivated and addresses an emerging multimodal task. The authors provided a detailed rebuttal clarifying annotation consistency, bias, quality control, and future extensions. Reviewers acknowledged these clarifications and generally agreed that their major concerns were addressed.

After rebuttal, all four reviewers updated or confirmed their scores to Borderline Accept (4). Importantly, none of the reviewers recommend a clear reject; rather, they see value in the dataset but did not show strong endorsement. The main reasons for hesitation are (1) the dataset scale and scope may still be limited compared to existing benchmarks, and (2) the technical novelty of the benchmark is incremental, making the overall impact somewhat less competitive relative to stronger submissions.

In summary, the submission sits at the borderline. While there is clear appreciation for the effort and potential usefulness of LISAt, the final decision may depend on the program’s overall acceptance rate and balance between dataset/benchmark contributions and other tracks.

I recommend discussing this paper at the SAC level to determine whether the collective borderline support suffices for acceptance this year.

author_final_remarks.value:
We thank the reviewers and ACs for their time and thoughtful feedback. We would like to note two points for awareness.

First, some of Reviewer aAGc’s comments reference terms and concepts (e.g., “interpreting 3D scenes based on natural language instructions,” “real-world robotic understanding,” “simulated environments,” “robotic navigation”) that are not part of our submission. These may have been mentioned in error, perhaps in reference to a different, robotics-focused paper. We nevertheless agree that discussing potential failure cases and including a responsible-use note is important for any AI system, and we will add such a note to our final submission.

Second, Reviewer nMAS did not provide a follow-up after our rebuttal, although we addressed all of the questions they had raised. We hope this context is helpful in the final evaluation.

We thank the reviewer for their thoughtful feedback and for highlighting these important ethical considerations. We share the reviewer's concerns regarding the potential for misuse of satellite imagery analysis and appreciate the opportunity to address them more thoroughly.

As the reviewer noted, we have included an initial discussion of these issues in our Impact Statement. We agree that a more detailed examination of the dual-use nature of this technology is warranted. To that end, we will expand our “Limitations and Failure Cases” section to create a more comprehensive “Limitations and Ethical Considerations” section as suggested.

The challenge of surveillance is inherent to many imaging technologies, including satellite data, and is not unique to our method. The goal of LISAt is to advance geospatial analysis for a wide range of applications, such as environmental monitoring and disaster response. We train on a dataset that the community has widely accepted to be benign (xView). We believe that the most effective way to mitigate the risks of misuse is to foster open and transparent research in this area, and we are committed to being a part of that conversation.

1) Many proprietary MLLMs, such as o1, GPT-4o, are not compared. Only geospatial-relation VLMs are used as baselines, which are not enough.

Thank you for your feedback, we have included evaluations from GPT‑4o and GPT-o1, showing that these models' performance with geospatial-relation VLMs across multistep geospatial reasoning tasks. The dataset used is the PreGRES test data, and we summarized all results compared with LISAt_pre in the table below. We note that since GPT-4o and GPT-o1 do not explicitly output segmentation masks, they cannot be fairly compared with LISAt, as a specialized prompt needs to be engineered to get the models to output coordinates of points in the contour lines for the target object.

are reported for BLEU-4 and CIDEr metrics.

Interestingly, GPT-4o and GPT-o1 yielded identical scores across all metrics and benchmark datasets. We verified that this results from both models returning generic or irrelevant outputs (e.g., hallucinated captions or answers unrelated to the query or blank), likely due to their lack of grounding in geospatial semantics and structured output generation.

While these models are state-of-the-art in general-purpose multimodal reasoning, they sometimes require crafted prompting strategies to perform meaningfully on domain-specific tasks like geospatial captioning or other domain-related VQA. This highlights the need for specialized VLMs like LISAt that natively support geospatial semantics and reasoning.

2) Although all datasets are geospatial datasets, the model design and training pipeline are very general, which do not reflect the uniqueness of geospatial data. Although the model performances are improved on many geospatial datasets, is this due to the domain adaptation? 

Thank you for your observation. While we framed our model architecture and training pipeline to be general-purpose because of the modularity that the design choice offers, the performance improvements on geospatial datasets primarily stem from the effective domain adaptation techniques that we employed in this work. These started from the dataset curation and include the careful selection of the vision and language encoder combination, as well as the vision backbone used.

2.1) How does LISAt perform on some natural image tasks? 

We evaluated the performance of the LISAt model on the natural images test set from the LISA benchmark (Lai et al., 2023). “LISA-7B on LISA Natural Images Data” is the baseline model reported in the original paper. “LISA-7B (ft)” refers to the fine-tuned version, where Lai et al. note that performance improves after fine-tuning on 239 complex-reasoning samples. “LISAt on LISA Natural Images Data” represents our LISAt model evaluated on the same test set, while “LISAt (Ours) on GRES Data” shows its performance on the GRES dataset.

| Type of Model and Data                               | cIoU   | gIoU  |
|----------------------------------------------------------|----------|---------|
| LISA-7B on LISA Natural Images Data        | 0.341 | 0.368 |
| LISA-7B (ft) on LISA Natural Images Data  | 0.484 | 0.473 |
| LISAt on LISA Natural Images Data            | 0.326 | 0.341 |
| LISAt (Ours) on GRES Data                        | 0.245 | 0.275 |

2.2) Will it be significantly worse?

The difference is expected, as LISAt is designed for generalization across geospatial and abstract reasoning segmentation tasks, and has not been fine-tuned on the LISA dataset. 1) Annotation Consistency and Bias: While the GRES dataset is high-quality, the annotation process may still be subject to semantic ambiguity or inconsistency, especially in multi-turn language instruction and complex urban scenes. The authors do not discuss inter-annotator agreement or error distributions.

Thank you for your feedback and for raising an important point. For the classes on the targeted object referenced in natural language in each image, we inherited from the `Quality Control and Gold Standards` method used in the xView paper [Liam et al, 2018] for the xView dataset. The authors of the xView dataset outline in their paper a three-tier quality assurance process: worker, supervisory, and expert stages. In the first stage, labelers reviewed each other’s annotations in a rotating manner. During the supervisory phase, the process included checks for duplicate or incorrect labels, geometry errors, incomplete annotation coverage, misaligned features, and empty image tiles. In the final expert stage, annotations were compared against a gold standard dataset. This reference dataset was developed by the paper’s co-authors and professional image analysts. It involves a manual labeling of six 1 km^2 image chips per batch. To meet the expert-level quality standard at this 3rd stage, annotation batches were required to achieve a minimum of 0.75 precision and 0.95 recall at a 0.5 Intersection over Union (IoU) threshold when evaluated against the gold standard.

For natural language queries, we generated three variations per RGB image and used cosine similarity to ensure they conveyed semantically equivalent information. Only those with a similarity/ alignment score of 0.9 or higher were retained.

Regarding ground truth segmentation masks produced via GeoSAM, we used only the cropped RGB regions defined by the bounding boxes in the xView dataset [Liam et al., 2018]. Random batches of GeoSAM outputs were inspected by co-authors in a rotating manner. Their task was to validate or reject the generated masks. A randomly selected data point from a random batch was retained only if all participants unanimously agreed on its accuracy.

We are actively working on reporting these in a table in our final submission.

2) Limited Temporal and Multimodal Context: Despite LISAt’s richness, the dataset focuses solely on static RGB imagery. Many real-world applications (e.g., disaster response, deforestation monitoring) benefit from temporal context, elevation data (DSM), or SAR modalities. The current dataset design does not support temporal grounding or reasoning, which restricts model generalization in spatiotemporal tasks.

Thank you for this observation. The use of temporal and multimodal context is part of our plan to build on this project. We view LISAt as a foundational step that will help build annotations for temporal sequences, where annotations for each frame will be obtained using the method employed in LISAt. Since we observe a promising scaling property in LISAt, we suspect that augmenting the dataset with more data (either temporal or additional modalities) will lead to improved performance, and we will be confirming this through further experimentation.

In out future work, we plan to gather geospatial temporal data and to investigate the impact of frame-rate downsampling as well as comparing models that use temporal vision encoders similar to TimeSformer (Bertasius et al, 2021) and ViViT (Arnab et al, 2021) combined with different language encoders to determine which combination generalizes best to spatiotemporal reasoning tasks. 

We also plan to investigate the impact of additional modalities such as elevation (DSM), and SAR, LIDAR modalities, in both static and temporal (needs to be gathered) settings, to assess their impact on performance. 

This direction aims to support richer temporal grounding and broaden the dataset’s applicability to dynamic, real-world geospatial scenarios.

1) Can LISAt be effectively applied to other types of images (such as aerial images or LiDAR data)? It is recommended to further verify its generalization ability. 

Thank you for the insightful suggestion. Evaluating LISAt’s performance on additional modalities such as SAR, LiDAR, and aerial imagery is indeed a valuable direction. Incorporating such modalities along with temporal data that will need to be gathered is part of our planned future work to enhance the generalization capacity of LISAt and expand the GRES dataset. We acknowledge the importance of verifying cross-modal generalization and intend to address this in future iterations of both the model and dataset.

2) Will the performance of LISAt decline when the query is vague or when multiple similar targets exist? 

Thank you for your question. While we assert that LISAt performs reasonably well even when the query is vague, as demonstrated in Table 5.2 (3rd row) and Table E16 (2nd row), there is room for improvement. We believe this can be addressed with more data, as evidenced by LISAt’s scalability behavior in Figure 4.4. Similarly, in cases with multiple similar targets in the images, while the model does not completely lose accuracy, additional data could further enhance performance, as shown in Table E19 (3rd and 4th rows). We also acknowledge these limitations in the manuscript (lines 296–299), where we mention that LISAt struggles when images are clouded, key features are obscured, or when queries are too vague, such as “Identify the plane in the bottom-right of the image,” where multiple objects occupy the same region.


3) If there are errors in GT, will it affect the accuracy of the assessment? 

Yes, we agree that while highly efficient, GeoSAM produces occasional inaccuracies in GT masks, which can negatively affect the model's performance. When the GT contains inaccuracies, the model is unfairly penalized, even if it correctly identifies the relevant features. As we mentioned in the manuscript (lines 301–303), the model's performance would likely have been higher if it weren’t for such discrepancies between the GT and model predictions, even though the model was performing as expected. We plan to address this in future iterations/ updates release versions of the dataset. 

3.1) How to solve this problem? 

As part of the improvements in future work, one potential solution is to reannotate and correct the mistakes generated by GeoSAM, using approaches such as iterative/ active learning. Specifically, we would fine-tune an open-source equivalent of GeoSAM on a different subset of the data to output GTs, which would then be corrected by human annotators if errors are observed. The corrected data could then be used to further fine-tune the model, and we would continue this process iteratively until the model outputs perfect masks.

Another approach worth exploring is to introduce confidence levels and assign weights to GT instances based on their confidence during the fine-tuning stage. For example, GT labels with higher certainty could be given more weight, while uncertain labels are treated with less importance.

4) Can the LISAt be applied to cloud layer occlusion, extreme weather, and noisy scenes? How robust is the model? 

Yes, LISAt does perform reasonably well in some cases involving cloud layer occlusion, extreme weather, and noisy scenes, as demonstrated in the 1st row of Table 5.2 and the 4th row of Table E15. However, we acknowledge that these scenarios remain challenging. As shown in Figure 4.4, performance improves with more data, suggesting that further scaling could lead to increased robustness under such adverse conditions. We have also discussed this limitation in the manuscript (lines 296–297), where we note that performance may degrade in scenes with heavy occlusion or low visibility.

5) How does LISAt perform in segmenting images of different resolutions? 
As reported in the table below, we observe that LISAt’s performance decreases as we go lower in resolution, which will be included in our final manuscript.

We agree that assessing inference speed and computational requirements is important for evaluating practical deployment feasibility. We have included an analysis in the table (above), which reports the average inference time per image-query pair on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU across different image resolutions.

For instance, at a standard resolution of 512×512, the model achieves 0.244 seconds per query, while maintaining competitive accuracy (cIoU: 0.245 ± 0.023, gIoU: 0.275 ± 0.009). As expected, inference becomes slower and less accurate at very low resolutions (e.g., 32×32), where performance drops (gIoU: 0.042 ± 0.004) and latency slightly increases (0.468s). 

We believe the inference time increases at lower resolutions because the frozen vision encoder still processes inputs at a fixed size of 512×512 in our case. This requires lower-resolution input images to the resized back to 512x512, which adds an overhead. These resized images also contain fewer details, which makes it harder for the model to perform well since our pipeline resizes all inputs to the fixed resolution required by the encoder before inference. 

For very small images (e.g., 32×32), the additional overhead from resizing operations and suboptimal GPU utilization can slightly increase inference time, as shown in the table.

This indicates that reducing input resolution significantly degrades visual quality without providing meaningful speed benefits, which supports the use of higher resolutions (e.g., 512×512) in deployment settings. 

We will add this discussion to our final submission.

1) The GRES dataset is entirely derived from the xView dataset. Although xView covers a variety of land object categories, this may introduce potential biases in terms of geographical location, sensor type, imaging season, and atmospheric conditions. The authors observed a plateau in performance in Figure 4.4 and correctly inferred the need for more diverse data. It is suggested that the authors more explicitly discuss this "source dataset bias" as a limitation in the paper and look forward to enriching GRES by integrating seed data from more sources.

Thank you for your recommendation. Although the xView dataset covers regions in South America, Africa, Europe, Asia, and Australia, we agree that the dataset would benefit from additional datasets from around the world, as shown in Figure 4.4. In our next iteration of this dataset, augmenting it with datasets such as SpaceNet (Etten et al., 2018) and COWC (Mundhenk et al., 2016) will be valuable.
Similarly, we plan for our future work to benefit from including sensor types, imaging seasons, and atmospheric conditions, as well as investigating temporal geospatial data. We will clarify this in the limitations section of our final manuscript and, as part of future work, explicitly state our plan to enrich GRES with seed data from additional datasets to address these biases and improve model robustness.

2) The architecture of the LISAt model largely follows the "embedding-as-a-mask" paradigm introduced by LISA. Its novelty lies more in the component selection for the remote sensing field, rather than fundamental architectural innovation. This is not a major issue in itself, as the core contribution of this paper is the dataset. However, to more accurately position the work, it is suggested that the authors more clearly state this in the introduction or model section, emphasizing that their work is a successful application of a mature framework to a new and more challenging geospatial domain through domain-specific data and component optimization.

Thank you for this feedback. We appreciate the suggestion and will make sure to clarify this point in the model section of our final manuscript. We agree that this distinction will help readers better understand the paper's core contribution in terms of both the dataset and the initial benchmark model application.

3) Using GPT-4v to generate queries is an effective strategy. However, is there a difference in language style and complexity between these queries generated by large models and real analysts' queries? Is there a risk that the model may overfit to "GPT-style" queries? If there could be a small-scale human evaluation, or a comparative analysis of GPT-generated queries and some real-world query samples, it would make the dataset construction process more convincing. This could be a secondary point of discussion or a direction for future work.

Thank you for your insightful comment. We agree that using GPT-generated queries is an effective strategy, but it is important to consider the potential differences in language style and complexity between those generated by large models and real analysts. 

To preliminarily investigate this, we conducted a small-scale comparative analysis using 10 test examples. We created two additional query variants: (1) human-like rewordings and (2) template-based queries referencing specific image regions. Our evaluation showed in the table below revealed that while GPT-style queries achieved slightly higher average performance on segmentation metrics, the differences were accompanied by relatively high variance, likely due to the tiny sample size.

This initial result suggests that GPT-generated queries are a reasonable proxy for human queries in the current setting, supporting the effectiveness of our dataset construction approach. However, we agree that a larger-scale collection of real human queries would provide a stronger validation and potentially improve the dataset further if augmented with such a collection. We plan to pursue this direction as part of our future work, as indicated in the revised manuscript.

We will ensure to explicitly discuss the limitations of GPT-style queries in the final manuscript, and discuss how our preliminary evaluation, along with the strong empirical results, demonstrates that GPT-generated queries provide a viable and effective foundation for training and evaluation in this context.

4) The experimental results show that the general SAM slightly outperforms GeoSAM, which is fine-tuned for geospatial data, in segmentation performance. The paper attributes this to SAM's broader training data, making its feature extraction more adaptable. Does this also imply that the supervised signal from fine-tuning on GRES is strong enough that a general model can be effectively adapted, thus making the domain-specific pretraining of GeoSAM less critical in this process?

Thank you for this insightful observation. We agree that the strong supervised signal from fine-tuning on GRES, combined with SAM’s more generalizable features, makes the domain-specific pretraining of GeoSAM less critical in this pipeline. While standalone GeoSAM was more effective in helping us extract ground truth masks when the bounding box of the target object was provided during dataset preparation, it does not deliver the same performance when combined with our LISAt Pre MLLM and the pipeline fine-tuned on GRES.

Considering practical deployment, it would make the work more complete if the authors could briefly discuss the inference speed and resource consumption of the LISAt model, as well as the possibility of creating lighter versions through techniques such as model distillation in the future.

In the table above, we report the average inference time (in seconds per image-query pair) for various input image sizes when running on a single A100 GPU.

summary.value:
The paper presents LISAt, a large-scale multimodal dataset and benchmark for language-grounded segmentation in satellite imagery. The dataset is composed of two parts:

1. GRES: A curated dataset of 9,205 high-resolution remote sensing images paired with 27,615 natural-language segmentation instructions and polygon annotations.

2. PreGRES: A large-scale pretraining dataset containing over 1 million language–image pairs aggregated from 12 existing remote sensing datasets.

LISAt aims to bridge the gap between language understanding and geospatial visual reasoning and provides new benchmarks and baseline models for referring segmentation in satellite imagery.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. Task Novelty and Relevance: LISAt introduces language-instructed segmentation in the geospatial domain, which is largely underexplored compared to natural image domains. It aligns closely with real-world applications like disaster response, urban planning, and environmental monitoring.

2. High-Quality Annotation Pipeline: GRES includes high-resolution aerial imagery annotated via multi-turn, natural language interactions leading to polygon-level segmentation masks. This goes beyond captioning and provides fine-grained visual grounding.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. Annotation Consistency and Bias: While the GRES dataset is high-quality, the annotation process may still be subject to semantic ambiguity or inconsistency, especially in multi-turn language instruction and complex urban scenes. The authors do not discuss inter-annotator agreement or error distributions.

2. Limited Temporal and Multimodal Context: Despite LISAt’s richness, the dataset focuses solely on static RGB imagery. Many real-world applications (e.g., disaster response, deforestation monitoring) benefit from temporal context, elevation data (DSM), or SAR modalities. The current dataset design does not support temporal grounding or reasoning, which restricts model generalization in spatiotemporal tasks.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

final_justification.value: The rebuttal addressed my concerns on annotation consistency, bias, and limitations in temporal/multimodal context. The explanation of the quality assurance process and future dataset expansion was convincing, and no major unresolved issues remain. I therefore maintain my Borderline Accept recommendation.

(4) Can the LISAT be applied to cloud layer occlusion, extreme weather, and noisy scenes? How robust is the model?
(5) How does LISAT perform in segmenting images of different resolutions? 
(6) The labels in the GRES dataset may not be accurate. Will this affect the evaluation effect of the model?
(7) It is suggested to incorporate an assessment of the inference speed and the required computing resources analysis, to ensure its feasibility in actual deployment.

summary.value: This paper addresses a problem in the field of geospatial artificial intelligence: reasoning segmentation of remote sensing images. The authors point out that existing vision-language models (VLMs) perform poorly when it comes to segmenting specific targets in satellite images based on complex, implicit natural language queries. To tackle this issue, the paper makes three core contributions: (i) a semi-synthetic geospatial reasoning segmentation dataset named GRES. (ii) a large-scale multimodal pretraining corpus, integrating multiple existing remote sensing datasets to gather over 1 million question-answer pair. (iii) A VLM-based benchmark model serving as a language-instructed segmentation assistant.

strengths_contributions.value:
- The most prominent contribution of this paper is the GRES and PreGRES datasets. The semi-automatic generation process of GRES is particularly ingenious and scalable. Integrating multiple existing datasets into PreGRES for pretraining also effectively enhances the model's generalization ability.
- The paper is well-written and well-structured. The authors are very candid in discussing the model's limitations and failure cases, such as difficulties in handling ambiguous queries and images with cloud cover, as well as cases where the model is unfairly penalized due to imperfect GT generated by GeoSAM. This transparency greatly enhances the credibility of the work.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- The GRES dataset is entirely derived from the xView dataset. Although xView covers a variety of land object categories, this may introduce potential biases in terms of geographical location, sensor type, imaging season, and atmospheric conditions. The authors observed a plateau in performance in Figure 4.4 and correctly inferred the need for more diverse data. It is suggested that the authors more explicitly discuss this "source dataset bias" as a limitation in the paper and look forward to enriching GRES by integrating seed data from more sources.
- The architecture of the LISAT model largely follows the "embedding-as-a-mask" paradigm introduced by LISA. Its novelty lies more in the component selection for the remote sensing field, rather than fundamental architectural innovation. This is not a major issue in itself, as the core contribution of this paper is the dataset. However, to more accurately position the work, it is suggested that the authors more clearly state this in the introduction or model section, emphasizing that their work is a successful application of a mature framework to a new and more challenging geospatial domain through domain-specific data and component optimization.
- Using GPT-4v to generate queries is an effective strategy. However, is there a difference in language style and complexity between these queries generated by large models and real analysts' queries? Is there a risk that the model may overfit to "GPT-style" queries? If there could be a small-scale human evaluation, or a comparative analysis of GPT-generated queries and some real-world query samples, it would make the dataset construction process more convincing. This could be a secondary point of discussion or a direction for future work.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

additional_feedback.value:
- The experimental results show that the general SAM slightly outperforms GeoSAM, which is fine-tuned for geospatial data, in segmentation performance. The paper attributes this to SAM's broader training data making its feature extraction more adaptable. Does this also imply that the supervised signal from fine-tuning on GRES is strong enough that a general model can be effectively adapted, thus making the domain-specific pretraining of GeoSAM less critical in this process? 
- On page 8, line 262, "Figure 4.1" is cited, but according to the context and content, it should refer to "Table 4.1".
- The paper mentions the computational resources required for training (8x A100 GPUs). Considering practical deployment, it would make the work more complete if the authors could briefly discuss the inference speed and resource consumption of the LISAT model, as well as the possibility of creating lighter versions through techniques such as model distillation in the future.

dataset_code_comments.value: The data can be downloaded from Huggingface, and the data loading and model training code can be found on Github.

ethical_comments.value: It is evident that there are no ethical concerns.

final_justification.value: After reviewing the authors’ response and the other reviewers’ comments, I’m satisfied that my concerns have been addressed. I’m keeping my original score and support accepting the paper.

title.value: LISAt: Language-Instructed Segmentation Assistant for Satellite Imagery

TLDR.value: A new multi-modal dataset and an initial  benchmark model for Geo-spatial Artificial Intelligence

abstract.value: Segmentation models can recognize a pre-defined set of objects in images. However, segmentation models capable of "reasoning" over complex user queries that implicitly refer to multiple objects of interest remain underexplored, especially in the geospatial domain. Recent advances in "reasoning segmentation"---generating segmentation masks from complex, implicit query text---demonstrate the potential of vision-language models (VLMs) to reason across an open domain of objects. Yet, our experiments reveal that these models struggle when applied to the unique challenges of remote-sensing imagery. To address this gap, we introduce a new dataset which consists of: GRES, a curated geospatial reasoning-segmentation dataset with 27,615 annotations across 9,205 images, and PreGRES, a collection of existing datasets to make up a large-scale multimodal pretraining corpus with over 1M question-answer pairs across 119,279 images. We propose an initial benchmark model, LISAt, a VLM for geospatial analysis that can describe complex remote-sensing scenes, answer detailed queries, and segment objects based on natural-language prompts. LISAt establishes a strong initial geospatial benchmark, outperforming prior foundation models such as RS-GPT4V by 10.04\% (BLEU-4) on visual description tasks and surpassing open-domain models on geospatial reasoning segmentation by 143.36\% (gIoU). Our model, dataset, and code are available on our project page: https://lisat-bair.github.io/LISAt/.
